problems.title: Museum Ticket Pair Count
problems.story: Museum Ticket Pair Count is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise distinct target pairs result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Museum Ticket Pair Count. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the distinct target pairs, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is the target. The remaining elements form the collection to pair.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of distinct unordered value pairs whose sum equals the target.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: A pair uses two different positions; equal-value pairs need two copies.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated distinct target pairs process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 3.
Example 2 follows the stated distinct target pairs process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.

testCases.explanation: Applying the distinct target pairs rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the distinct target pairs rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Sort the collection and place one pointer at each end.
Move both pointers after a match and skip repeated values so a value pair is counted once.

editorial.overview: Sort the payload values, then converge two pointers according to whether their sum is below, above, or equal to the target.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every pair of positions and store matching value pairs in a set to remove duplicates.
editorial.optimalApproach: A sorted two-pointer scan counts each distinct complement pair once while skipping equal neighbors.
editorial.correctnessProof: At each step, a sum below target cannot be repaired by decreasing the right value, so advancing left loses no solution; the symmetric argument holds above target. A match is counted once and duplicate values are skipped, so every distinct pair appears exactly once.

c11.functionSignature: long long solve(const long long *values, int n)

serialization.input: Whitespace-separated signed integers read into values.

c11.referenceSolution:
int cmp_ll(const void*a,const void*b){long long x=*(const long long*)a,y=*(const long long*)b;return x>y?1:x<y?-1:0;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(n<3)return 0;long long*a=malloc(sizeof(long long)*(n-1));memcpy(a,v+1,sizeof(long long)*(n-1));qsort(a,n-1,sizeof(long long),cmp_ll);int l=0,r=n-2;long long c=0;while(l<r){long long s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;long long x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}free(a);return c;}

serialization.input: Whitespace-separated signed integers read into values.

python3.referenceSolution:
def solve(v: list[int]) -> int:
    if not v: return 0
    t,a=v[0],sorted(v[1:]);l,r,c=0,len(a)-1,0
    while l<r:
        s=a[l]+a[r]
        if s==t:
            c+=1;x,y=a[l],a[r]
            while l<r and a[l]==x:l+=1
            while l<r and a[r]==y:r-=1
        elif s<t:l+=1
        else:r-=1
    return c

serialization.input: Whitespace-separated signed integers read into values.

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){if(!v.length)return 0;const t=v[0],a=v.slice(1).sort((x,y)=>x-y);let l=0,r=a.length-1,c=0;while(l<r){const s=a[l]+a[r];if(s===t){c++;const x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]===x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]===y)r--;}else if(s<t)l++;else r--;}return c;}

problems.title: Ferry Weight Rating
problems.story: A vehicle ferry runs a fixed number of crossings a day. Vehicles wait on the slipway in a single queue and board strictly in that order, because the queue is the fairness rule and nobody is waved past anyone else. Each crossing takes as many vehicles from the front as will fit, then sails. The operator is buying a replacement ferry and has to state a weight rating: too small and the queue will not clear by nightfall, too large and they are paying for a boat they do not need.
problems.statement:
You are given the number of crossings available and the weight of each vehicle in queue order.

Every vehicle must cross today. Vehicles board in queue order, so each crossing carries a run of vehicles taken from the front of what remains. A crossing may carry any number of vehicles as long as their combined weight does not exceed the ferry rating.

Return the smallest weight rating that gets every vehicle across within the available crossings.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is how many crossings the ferry can make today. Every number after it is the weight of one vehicle in kilograms, in the order the vehicles stand in the queue.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest weight rating that clears the whole queue within the available crossings.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The number of crossings available, followed by the weight of each vehicle in queue order.

constraints: The queue holds n = values.length - 1 vehicles, and 1 <= crossings <= n
The answer can exceed the range of a 32-bit signed integer: one crossing carrying a full queue may total 200000000000000

examples.explanation: With a rating of 70 the crossings carry 40 and 30, then 50 and 20, then 60 and 10, which is three crossings exactly. A rating of 69 forces the first crossing to take only the 40, and the queue no longer clears in three.
Six crossings for six vehicles means each can sail alone, so the rating only has to carry the heaviest single vehicle. No rating below 60 works at all, because that vehicle could never board.
One crossing must carry the entire queue, so the rating is the total weight of every vehicle waiting.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: three crossings of 70 kilograms each.
A single crossing, so the rating is the whole queue at once.
The smallest legal input: one crossing and one vehicle. Catches a search whose bounds collapse wrongly when they start equal.
One crossing carrying three vehicles at the maximum weight. The answer exceeds a 32-bit signed integer, and so does the upper bound of the search.
One crossing per vehicle, so the answer is the heaviest single vehicle.
Six identical vehicles over three crossings, two per crossing. Catches an off-by-one that returns 13 and leaves a vehicle behind.

The lower-bound trap. Total weight is 104 over five crossings, so a search starting from the average of 21 returns a rating that the 100 kilogram vehicle could never board on. The search must start at the heaviest single vehicle.
Five vehicles over two crossings splits three and two, so the rating is 15 rather than the 13 an even division of the total would suggest.

hints: A bigger ferry never makes the queue harder to clear. Convince yourself of that first, because everything else depends on it.
For a rating you have already picked, counting the crossings it needs is easy: fill each one from the front until the next vehicle will not fit, then sail.
That counting test answers yes for every rating above some threshold and no for every rating below it. The answer is exactly that threshold.
The candidate ratings are not in the input. They run from some lowest sensible rating up to the total weight of the queue, and you are searching that range rather than the array.
The lowest sensible rating is not the average load per crossing. A vehicle heavier than the rating can never board at all, so the range starts at the heaviest single vehicle.

editorial.overview: The queue order is fixed and every crossing takes a run from the front, so a rating determines the whole schedule: fill each crossing until the next vehicle will not fit. That makes the number of crossings a function of the rating alone, and the question becomes finding the smallest rating whose crossing count fits the budget.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every candidate rating from the heaviest vehicle upward and stop at the first that clears the queue in time. Each trial costs one sweep of the queue. It is correct and hopeless: the range of candidates reaches two hundred billion thousand, so even at one sweep per candidate this never finishes.
editorial.optimalApproach: Binary search the rating. The search space is not the input array but the interval from the heaviest single vehicle up to the total weight of the queue, because no smaller rating can carry the heaviest vehicle and no larger rating is ever needed. For a candidate rating, sweep the queue once with a running load, starting a new crossing whenever the next vehicle would overflow, and compare the crossings used against the budget. If it fits, the answer is at most this rating, so move the upper bound down to it; otherwise move the lower bound above it. The loop ends with the bounds equal on the smallest rating that fits. One sweep per step gives O(n log S) time, where S is the total weight, and O(1) extra space.
editorial.correctnessProof: The greedy sweep is optimal for a fixed rating. Suppose some schedule uses fewer crossings than the sweep. Compare them from the front: the sweep puts at least as many vehicles on the first crossing as any valid schedule can, because it only stops when the next vehicle would overflow, so after the first crossing the sweep has cleared a prefix at least as long. Repeating the argument, the sweep is never behind after any crossing, so it cannot finish later. Therefore the crossings it counts is the true minimum for that rating. Monotonicity follows: raising the rating never causes the sweep to start a crossing earlier, so the crossing count never increases. The predicate is therefore false below a threshold and true at and above it, which is exactly what binary search needs, and the bounds are valid because the heaviest vehicle must fit on some crossing and the total weight always fits in one.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log S), where n is the number of vehicles and S the total weight. One sweep of the queue per binary-search step.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the input, since the sweep only carries a running load and a count.

provenance.author: Vikram Yadav
provenance.note: Fourth hand-authored replacement for the generated library described in D27, written against docs/authoring-problems.md. Binary searching over an answer space with a greedy feasibility predicate is a standard technique and is named openly in the editorial; the story, wording, example values and test cases are original to this record. Labelled hard rather than medium because the existing binary-search group searches inside the given array, while this one requires constructing a search space that appears nowhere in the input and proving the predicate monotone. The counter-argument, that binary search is the topic’s own tool and so should not count as a step up, is recorded here because the call is close.
